evidence_quotes.quote: This paper explores the different urban governance models proposed by multilateral aid organizations in accessing water through informal supply systems, to assess the rationale and the guiding principles at the basis of their different ‘governance approaches’.

After briefly outlying the evolving relationship between urban governance and the delivery of urban services, this paper explores the three selected multilateral aid organizations’ position in regards to the recognition and regulation of informal providers involved in urban drinking water delivery.

The theoretical framework applied in this paper relies on the idea of ‘evaluation models’ in accessing urban water services, where an evaluation model represents the values carried out by the different paradigms developed in accessing drinking water (Baron, 2005).

As a result, the relevant evidence applied in this paper relies on the few theoretical and empirical documents and reports that the multilateral aid organizations considered have been recently producing, with regards to the specific issue of informal water supply systems.

All the same it is important to highlight that, despite the relevance of the water sector in the international development cooperation, this investigation is based on the evidence of the available documentation produced by the aid organizations considered and explicitly related to the specific paper’s issue of informal water supply systems.

criterion_notes.c1: Thematically addresses access to urban drinking water supply services in developing countries via informal water supply systems and small-scale providers.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording: YES — the paper examines urban governance approaches and multilateral donor policy stances regarding the recognition, formalization, and regulation of informal water providers. Narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: NO — although sections 4.3, 5.3, and 6.3 discuss donor views on legal status, provider exclusivity, and formalization of small-scale providers in the abstract, the paper analyzes broad multilateral donor macro-governance ideologies ('market-based' vs. 'general interest' guiding principles) rather than how a concrete legal or administrative rule-type mechanism operates to govern household or community water access. Note that even under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the study is still excluded (plain_criterion2_decision = exclude) because it fails Criteria 3, 4, and 5.
criterion_notes.c3: NO — this is a narrative policy overview and conceptual essay comparing selected policy/strategy documents from three multilateral aid organizations (World Bank, UN-HABITAT, and the European Commission) against Baron's (2005) normative 'evaluation models' typology. It has no empirical research design or methods section, collects no primary quantitative or qualitative data, and is not a systematic empirical synthesis (exclude as E05).
criterion_notes.c4: NO — the paper evaluates the normative guiding principles ('market-based' vs. 'general interest' evaluation models) expressed in donor policy documents and reports no primary or systematically synthesized empirical outcome on household or community water access, connection, reliability, continuity, quantity, affordability, or exclusion.
criterion_notes.c5: NO — the unit of analysis is the policy discourse of three international donor agencies rather than an empirical population exposed to a governance mechanism with a measured service-access outcome, and no empirical study design is identifiable.

study_design: Narrative policy overview / conceptual review of donor policy documents (non-empirical)
population_and_sample: Three multilateral aid organizations (World Bank, UN-HABITAT, and the European Union/European Commission) and their selected policy and strategy documents on informal urban water supply
exposure: Urban governance models and policy positions of multilateral aid organizations regarding informal water supply providers and community-based arrangements
outcome: Normative guiding principles ('market-based' vs. 'general interest' evaluation models) underlying multilateral donor policy discourse (no empirical service access outcome reported)
rationale: Excluded under E05 (No empirical evidence). Moretto (2007) is a narrative policy overview and conceptual commentary comparing the normative 'guiding principles' ('market-based' vs. 'general interest' evaluation models) of three multilateral aid organizations (World Bank, UN-HABITAT, and the European Union) toward informal urban water supply systems based on selected institutional reports and policy documents. It employs no empirical methodology, presents no primary data or systematic empirical synthesis, and reports no empirical household or community water access outcomes. In addition, under the 2026-10-13 narrow reading of Criterion 2, it focuses on high-level donor macro-governance paradigms rather than analyzing an operational rule-type mechanism governing service access (though even under the plain reading of Criterion 2 it remains excluded for lack of empirical evidence and access outcomes).
